title: Rainwater collection from a roof
summary: Catch rain off a roof into covered tanks, with a first-flush diverter that sends the dirtiest water away and screens that keep out leaves and mosquitoes. A 50 m² roof catches about 40 L for every millimetre of rain, so a 10 mm shower fills a 400 L tank. Rainwater must still be filtered and boiled or disinfected before drinking.

materials.item: Tanks: food-grade drums, IBC totes, or water tanks, opaque and lidded
Gutters: existing, or made from split plastic pipe or bent sheet metal
Pipe: 50–100 mm downpipe or hose from gutter to tank, a 75–100 mm first-flush pipe with end cap and small drip hole, and an overflow pipe as big as the inlet (food-safe if you will drink the water)
Fine mesh (fly screen) for inlets and overflow
Tap or valve for the tank outlet, food-safe if you will drink the water
Base: compacted gravel, blocks or a strong timber platform
Tarp for a camp catchment instead of a roof

steps.text: Check the roof. Metal, glazed tile or plastic is good. Avoid tar or bitumen roofs, treated wood shingles, fresh paint, lead flashing and roofs under trees or heavy bird use.
steps.warn: Old grey corrugated cement roofs may contain asbestos. Don't cut, drill, scrub or walk on them; collect from them only as they are.

steps.text: Work out how much you'll catch and size the tanks with the notes.
Fix or make gutters with a slight fall (2–5 mm per metre) towards the outlet. Fit a coarse leaf screen at the top of the downpipe.
steps.warn: Work from a ladder with someone footing it. Never lean out sideways; move the ladder.

steps.text: Make the first-flush diverter: a vertical pipe teed off the downpipe before the tank. It fills first with the dirtiest water, then the rest flows on to the tank. Size it at about 1 L per m² of roof. A small drip hole or a removable cap at the bottom lets it empty between showers.
Prepare the base: level, firm, and big enough for the tank's footprint. Water weighs 1 kg per litre.
steps.warn: A full 1,000 L tank weighs a tonne. If it's on a stand, the stand must carry that safely, or it can collapse and crush.

steps.text: Clean the tanks. Use only containers that held food, drinks or water. Fit a screened inlet in the lid (mesh 1 mm or finer stops mosquitoes).
Fit the tap 10–15 cm above the tank bottom so sediment stays behind. Seal with washers both sides.
Fit an overflow near the top, as big as the inlet, screened at the end, leading away from the tank base and building foundations.
Connect downpipe → first flush → tank inlet. Link several tanks with a pipe between their bottoms, or overflow from one into the next.
Treat drinking water every time: filter it, then boil it or add plain bleach (2 drops of 5–6% per litre, wait 30 minutes). Use untreated rainwater only for washing and gardens.
steps.warn: Rainwater from roofs carries bird droppings, dust and germs. It is not safe to drink untreated.

steps.text: After each rain empty the first flush. Every month clean gutters and screens and check for mosquito larvae. Every year empty and clean the tanks.

notes:
## How much you catch
Litres = roof area (m², measured flat as seen from above) × rain (mm) × 0.8.
- 50 m² roof, 10 mm shower: 50 × 10 × 0.8 = 400 L.
- 50 m² roof, 800 mm a year: about 32,000 L a year.

## How big a tank
- Drinking and cooking: 3–5 L per person per day. Washing: 10–20 L more.
- Size the tank to carry you through the longest usual dry spell: litres per day × dry days.
- Several smaller tanks can be moved, cleaned and repaired one at a time.

## First flush
The first 0.5–2 mm of rain washes dust, droppings and leaves off the roof. At about 1 L per m² of roof, a 50 m² roof needs a 50 L diverter: about 7 m of 100 mm pipe, or a drum with a float ball that seals the inlet when full. For smaller volumes, a 2 m length of 100 mm pipe holds about 16 L.

## Keeping water good
- Opaque tanks stop algae. Paint or wrap clear tanks.
- Keep lids on and screens intact. Mosquito larvae appear within a week in open water.
- Draw from the tap, not by dipping buckets.
- Frost can split pipes and taps. Drain exposed parts in winter.

## What filtering and boiling do
- Settling and cloth or sand filters remove grit, leaves and some germs.
- Boiling (a rolling boil for 1 minute) or bleach kills germs.
- Neither removes chemicals from a contaminated roof, such as old paint or nearby smoke. Choose clean surfaces.

## Tarp catchment
A tarp tied at the corners with one corner lower, draining into a container, catches about 0.8 L per m² for each mm of rain. Good for camps and travel.

## If you lack a part
- No gutters: hang a sloped tarp or sheet metal strip under the roof edge, or cut a plastic drum in half lengthwise.
- No tap: siphon with a hose, or fit a short hose with a clamp.
